passage: Thursday. Went to Ammamma's room after dinner with the camp form still in my bag. She asked why I looked like a wet cat. I told her Papa wants me at the shop in June. She was quiet, then said, “At sixteen I gave up my place at the teachers' college to help my father in the fields.” I hadn't known that. “I don't regret helping him, kanna. I regret never telling him what it cost me. He would have found some way.” She said duty and growing up aren't two doors where you must close one; over a whole life you keep walking back and forth between them. She told me to say my piece first, and decide after. I feel steadier. Tomorrow I'll talk to Papa. (Ammamma's tea is still terrible.) — Pallavi

qa.q: What could Pallavi do next, and why?
qa.a: Pallavi could talk to Papa openly before deciding, since Ammamma's story shows that hiding the cost takes away the family's chance to find another way.

qa.q: How might Papa see Pallavi's silence if it continued?
qa.a: Papa might assume everything is fine and never see what Pallavi would give up, just as Ammamma's father never knew.

subtype: Approach: consulting an elder for perspective [Action]
passage:
In Mandsaur, Sangeeta had been asked to skip the district hockey trials to help her parents with the garlic harvest. She walked to her grandmother's house at the edge of the village, where Yamini Bai sat shelling peas on the verandah.

"You look like a storm," her grandmother said.

Sangeeta told her. Her grandmother was quiet for a while. Then she said, "When I was your age, I was offered a place at the teachers' training school in Indore. The same harvest problem. I stayed home."

"Do you regret it?"

"Some days. I became a good farmer. I raised your father well. But I never stood in a classroom." She handed Sangeeta a handful of pods. "Duty isn't one season, beti. Your life is long. Talk to your father. Maybe you help with the harvest after the trials."

Sangeeta walked home slowly, feeling less alone in the choice.

qa.q: What was young Yamini Bai offered?
qa.a: A place at the teachers' training school in Indore.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel walking home?
qa.a: She felt less alone and calmer, having heard someone else's version of the same choice.

qa.q: What small step could Sangeeta take next?
qa.a: She could ask her father whether she can join the harvest right after the trials, so both needs are met in turn.

qa.q: How does Yamini Bai look back on her own choice?
qa.a: She has mixed feelings: some regret about never teaching, but also pride in being a good farmer and raising her son well.

grounding: Shows a student talking with a grandmother who shares her own similar choice and its regrets, offering a longer view of balancing duty and growth.
